mainTopic: Wordings and disputed claims of freeing a slave or giving a field, and the משנה of a pledged slave (אפותיקי) who was freed
overview: The amud opens with the last line of an earlier discussion: the slave jingles coins before his master, and a גט שחרור is written for him. Two parallel ברייתות follow. Past or present wording ('I made him free,' 'I gave the field') works. Future wording ('I will...') is a מחלוקת, and רבי יוחנן adds that all these cases only work in a written שטר. Another pair of ברייתות covers a giver who says he freed a slave or gave a field while the other person denies it. A general claim stands, because it may have been done through someone else. A claim of personally handing over the document is overruled by the denial, since a person's own admission is like 100 witnesses. רב חסדא and רבה discuss who eats the disputed field's produce, and the גמרא explains they are talking about different cases: the father himself, or his son. Then a new משנה teaches that a slave pledged as אפותיקי and then freed owes nothing by strict law. Because of תיקון העולם, though, his master is forced to free him and the slave writes a note for his value, while רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says there is no note. The גמרא explains, using רבא's rule that שחרור cancels a lien, and begins explaining the תיקון העולם worry, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The slave jingles coins and a release document is written
steps.stepSummary: The end of an earlier discussion: the slave jingles money in front of his master, and a גט שחרור is written for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the slave jingles coins in front of him, and a document of freedom is written for him in his name.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last line of a discussion that began before this section. It finishes the practical advice: the slave jingles coins before his master, and a גט שחרור is written for the slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Jingling the coins makes the master want the money, so he agrees to the slave buying his freedom. Then a proper גט שחרור is written in the slave's name, so the release is done correctly in writing.

keyTerms.meaning: A document of freedom (גט שחרור) for a slave
In his name, written specifically for him

phrases.english: And he jingles coins before him,
phrases.notes: The slave rattles the money in front of his master so the master will want it and agree to free him.

phrases.aramaic: וְכָתֵב לֵיהּ גִּיטָּא דְחֵירוּתָא עַל שְׁמֵיהּ.
phrases.english: and a document of freedom is written for him in his name.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a discussion that started before this section.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The slave's release is done by giving the master money and writing a proper גט שחרור in the slave's name.

steps.title: Past or present wording frees the slave
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that saying 'I made my slave free,' 'he was made free,' or 'he is free' makes the slave a בן חורין.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: One who says, 'I made so-and-so my slave a free man,' or 'He was made a free man,' or 'He is a free man,' then he is a free man.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about the words a master uses to free his slave. Three wordings, past tense or present tense, all work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each of these wordings describes the freedom as something that already happened or is true right now. So the slave is free. The next step shows what happens with future wording.

keyTerms.meaning: A free man (no longer a slave)
Behold he is, he is now

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: One who says:
'I made so-and-so my slave a free man';
'He was made a free man';
'He is a free man' –
he is a free man.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן, הָאוֹמֵר: עָשִׂיתִי פְּלוֹנִי עַבְדִּי בֶּן חוֹרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: which words of release take effect.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Past-tense or present-tense wording of release makes the slave free.

steps.title: Future wording: רבי and the חכמים argue
steps.stepSummary: If the master says 'I will make him free,' רבי says the slave acquires his freedom, and the חכמים say he does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he says, 'I will make him a free man,' רבי says: He has acquired. The חכמים say: He has not acquired.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא goes on to future-tense wording, 'I will make him free.' Here there is a מחלוקת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי treats 'I will make him free' as enough to free the slave. The חכמים say it only sounds like a plan for later, so the slave is not freed by it. That is the difference from the past and present wordings in step 2, which everyone agrees work.

keyTerms.meaning: He did not acquire, it did not take effect

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with step 2. Everyone agrees that past and present wordings work. The מחלוקת is only about future wording, 'I will make him free.'

phrases.english: 'I will make him a free man' –
Rabbi says: He has acquired,
phrases.notes: Just 'רבי' with no other name means רבי יהודה הנשיא.

phrases.english: and the Sages say: He has not acquired.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, moving from past or present wording to future wording.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For future wording, רבי says the slave goes free and the חכמים say he does not.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: all of these only work in writing
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that every case in the ברייתא is talking about a written שטר, not just spoken words.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: And all of them are with a document.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן adds a key detail to the whole ברייתא. Every one of these wordings works only when it is written in a שטר given to the slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just saying 'he is free' out loud does not free a slave. You need a written שטר. So the ברייתא is not asking whether speech alone works. It is asking which wording inside a שטר works.

keyTerms.meaning: And all of them (all the cases listed)

steps.whyThisMatters: This changes how we read the whole ברייתא: the argument is about the wording inside a שטר, not about speaking out loud.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
And all of them are with a document.
phrases.notes: He means all the cases in the ברייתא, including the ones everyone agrees on.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the setting of the ברייתא in steps 2 and 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All the release wordings in the ברייתא only work when written in a שטר.

steps.title: Past or present wording gives away a field
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא teaches the same pattern for a gift of land: 'I gave,' 'it is given,' or 'it is his' all transfer the field.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: One who says, 'I gave such-and-such field to so-and-so,' or 'It is given to so-and-so,' or 'It is his,' then it is his.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא with the same structure, now about giving someone a field as a gift. Past and present wordings work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just like freeing a slave, wording that describes the gift as already done or true right now gives the field to the receiver. This sets up the same future-tense question in the next step.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: One who says:
'I gave such-and-such field to so-and-so';
'It is given to so-and-so';
'It is his' –
it is his.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן, הָאוֹמֵר: נָתַתִּי שָׂדֶה פְּלוֹנִית לִפְלוֹנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel ברייתא that applies the same wording pattern to a gift of land.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Past-tense or present-tense wording of a gift transfers the field.

steps.title: Future wording for a field: רבי מאיר and the חכמים argue
steps.stepSummary: If the owner says 'I will give it to so-and-so,' רבי מאיר says the receiver acquires the field, and the חכמים say he does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he says, 'I will give it to so-and-so,' רבי מאיר says: He has acquired. The חכמים say: He has not acquired.
steps.whatsHappening: Again the ברייתא moves to future wording, and again there is a מחלוקת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר holds that 'I will give it' is enough to transfer the field, like רבי in the slave case. The חכמים hold that it only sounds like a plan for the future, so the field does not transfer.

phrases.english: 'I will give it to so-and-so' –
Rabbi Meir says: He has acquired;
and the Sages say: He has not acquired.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the field ברייתא with the future-tense case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For future wording of a gift, רבי מאיר says the receiver acquires and the חכמים say he does not.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the field cases also only work in writing
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says the same thing about the field ברייתא: every case is talking about a written שטר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: And all of them are with a document.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן repeats his rule for the field ברייתא. These gift wordings only work when written in a שטר given to the receiver.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just saying 'I gave it to him' out loud does not transfer the field. You need a written שטר. So here too the מחלוקת is about which wording inside a שטר works.
steps.whatToRemember: In both a slave's release and a gift of a field, past or present wording works, and future wording ('I will...') is a מחלוקת. רבי יוחנן says all these cases only work in a written שטר.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
And all of them are with a document.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבי יוחנן's rule from step 4 to the field ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All the gift wordings for a field only work when written in a שטר.

steps.title: Master says he freed his slave, but the slave denies it
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if a master says 'I freed my slave' and the slave denies it, the slave is free, because the master may have done it through someone else. If the master says 'I wrote and handed him a שטר' and the slave denies it, the slave's own admission wins.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If someone says, 'I made so-and-so my slave a free man,' and the slave says, 'He did not make me free,' we worry that maybe the master gave him his freedom through another person. But if the master says, 'I wrote a שטר and handed it to him,' and the slave says, 'He did not write it for me and did not give it to me,' then a person's own admission is worth as much as 100 witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about a master and slave who disagree on whether the slave was freed. It gives two versions of the master's claim, and each version gets a different result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version the master speaks generally, so he could have freed the slave through someone else without the slave knowing. That is why the slave's denial means nothing and he goes free. In the second version the master says he personally handed the שטר to the slave, so the slave himself would know. The slave's statement 'I never got it' is an admission against himself, and a person's admission about himself is fully believed.

keyTerms.meaning: We are concerned; we take the possibility seriously
He gave him the benefit through another person
A person's admission about his own case

steps.confusionAlert: The slave's denial counts in the second case only. In the first case he could simply be unaware, so his denial proves nothing.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: One who says:
'I made so-and-so my slave a free man,'
and he (the slave) says: 'He did not make me (free)'

phrases.aramaic: חָיְישִׁינַן שֶׁמָּא זִיכָּה לוֹ עַל יְדֵי אַחֵר.
phrases.english: we are concerned that perhaps he gave it to him through another person.
phrases.notes: The slave might not know about it. That is why his denial doesn't stop him from being free.

phrases.english: (If the master says:) 'I wrote and I gave it to him,'

phrases.aramaic: וְהוּא אוֹמֵר: ״לֹא כָּתַב לִי וְלֹא נָתַן לִי״ –
phrases.english: and he says: 'He did not write for me and did not give me'

phrases.aramaic: הוֹדָאַת בַּעַל דִּין כְּמֵאָה עֵדִים דָּמֵי.
phrases.english: the admission of a party to the case is like 100 witnesses.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן, הָאוֹמֵר: עָשִׂיתִי פְּלוֹנִי עַבְדִּי בֶּן חוֹרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the wording of freeing a slave to a new question: what happens when the master and the slave disagree about whether it happened.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A general claim of freeing makes the slave free despite his denial. A claim of personally handing over the שטר is overruled by the slave's own denial.

steps.title: Owner says he gave a field, but the receiver denies it
steps.stepSummary: The same ברייתא repeats the pattern for a field. A general claim of giving counts because it may have been done through someone else. A claim of handing over a document is overruled by the receiver's own denial.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says, 'I gave such-and-such field to so-and-so,' and that person says, 'He did not give it to me,' we worry that maybe he gave it to him through another person. But if he says, 'I wrote and handed him a document,' and the other says, 'He did not write it and did not give it to me,' then a person's own admission is like 100 witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with the same two-part pattern, this time about giving away a field. This setup also prepares for the question about the field's produce that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Giving a field is a benefit, so it can be done for someone through another person without him knowing. That is why the general claim stands even though he denies it. When the giver says he personally handed over the document, the receiver would know, so his denial is an admission against himself and decides the case.

phrases.english: One who says: 'I gave such-and-such field to so-and-so,'
and he says: 'He did not give it to me'

phrases.aramaic: חָיְישִׁינַן שֶׁמָּא זִיכָּה לוֹ עַל יְדֵי אַחֵר.
phrases.english: we are concerned that perhaps he gave it to him through another person.
(If he says:) 'I wrote and I gave it to him,'

phrases.aramaic: וְהוּא אוֹמֵר: ״לֹא כָּתַב וְלֹא נָתַן לִי״ –
phrases.english: and he says: 'He did not write and did not give me'

phrases.aramaic: הוֹדָאַת בַּעַל דִּין כְּמֵאָה עֵדִים דָּמֵי.
phrases.english: the admission of a party to the case is like 100 witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same two rules from the slave case to a gift of a field, just as Steps 5 to 7 matched the slave wording with the field wording.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A general claim of giving transfers the field despite the receiver's denial. A claim of personally handing over the document is overruled by the receiver's denial.

steps.title: Who eats the produce of the disputed field?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks who gets to eat the field's produce while the giver says it was given and the receiver says it wasn't.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical follow-up question about the field case. This sets up the dispute that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the ברייתא's ruling the field may belong to the receiver, but the receiver himself says it is not his. So it is unclear who should actually enjoy what the field grows until things are cleared up.

phrases.english: Who eats the produce?
phrases.notes: This refers to the first field case, where the giver says 'I gave it' and the receiver says 'I never got it.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks a practical question that grows out of the field case in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who is entitled to eat the produce while ownership is disputed.

steps.title: רב חסדא says the giver eats it, and רבה says it is held aside
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא says the giver keeps eating the produce. רבה says the produce is put aside with a third person.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: The giver eats the produce. And רבה said: We put the produce aside with a third person.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים answer the question, and their answers seem to disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא leaves the produce with the giver, since the receiver says the field isn't his. רבה is more careful: since the field might belong to the receiver after all, nobody eats the produce yet, and it is held by a neutral person until the truth comes out.

keyTerms.meaning: We put it with a third person until things are clear

phrases.aramaic: רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר: נוֹתֵן אוֹכֵל פֵּירוֹת;
phrases.english: רב חסדא said: The giver eats the produce;
and רבה said: We place the produce with a third person.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר: נוֹתֵן אוֹכֵל פֵּירוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives two answers to the question in Step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב חסדא: the giver eats the produce. רבה: the produce is held by a third person.

steps.title: They do not argue: one case is about the father, the other about his son
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the two opinions do not really argue. One is about the receiver himself (the father), and the other is about the receiver's son.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they do not argue. This one is about the father, and that one is about the son.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the apparent disagreement by showing that each אמורא is talking about a different situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the father, the person who was supposed to receive the field, is alive and says 'it isn't mine,' the giver eats the produce. That is רב חסדא's case. When the son speaks after the father's death, he might simply not know that his father received the field, so the produce is held aside. That is רבה's case.

keyTerms.meaning: This one ... that one; pointing to two different cases

steps.whatToRemember: A general claim of giving counts even if the other person denies it. A claim of personally handing over the document is overruled by the receiver's denial. In the field case, the giver eats the produce when the father himself denies it, and the produce is held aside when it is the son who denies it.

phrases.english: And they do not argue:
this one is about the father, that one is about the son.
phrases.notes: The 'father' is the person who was supposed to get the field. The 'son' is his child, speaking after him, who might not know what his father received.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא פְּלִיגִי: הָא בְּאַבָּא, הָא בִּבְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the apparent dispute in Step 11 by giving each opinion its own case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each opinion applies to a different situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב חסדא and רבה seemed to disagree about the very same case.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב חסדא is talking about the father who denies receiving the field. רבה is talking about the son, who might not know.

steps.title: New משנה: a pledged slave who was freed
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a slave pledged as אפותיקי and then freed owes nothing by strict law. Because of תיקון העולם, the master is forced to free him formally, and the slave writes a note for his value.
steps.simpleTranslation: A master set aside his slave as guaranteed payment for a debt to someone else, and then he freed the slave. By strict law the slave owes nothing. But to make the world work better, the master is forced to make him free, and the slave writes a note promising to pay his value.
steps.whatsHappening: A brand-new משנה opens. It describes a slave who was pledged to a lender and then freed by his master.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two layers here. By strict law (שורת הדין), freeing the slave wipes out the lender's claim on him. The חכמים add a fix for the good of society (תיקון העולם): the freeing is made complete, and the slave takes on a debt equal to his own value.

keyTerms.meaning: An item set aside as the specific guaranteed payment for a debt
The strict letter of the law
An enactment of the חכמים to make society run properly

steps.confusionAlert: Only the lender is owed money here. The debt was the master's, but it is the freed slave who writes the note for his own value, to pay the lender.

phrases.aramaic: מַתְנִי׳ עֶבֶד שֶׁעֲשָׂאוֹ רַבּוֹ אַפּוֹתֵיקֵי לַאֲחֵרִים,
phrases.english: MISHNA: A slave whose master made him a designated payment for others,
phrases.notes: 'Others' means the people the master borrowed money from.

phrases.english: and then he freed him: by the letter of the law
the slave owes nothing at all;
but because of the betterment of the world,
we force his master
and he makes him a free man,
and he writes a note for his value.
phrases.notes: The one writing is the slave. He promises to pay the amount he was worth.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ עֶבֶד שֶׁעֲשָׂאוֹ רַבּוֹ אַפּוֹתֵיקֵי לַאֲחֵרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the previous discussion about claims of freeing and giving.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: By strict law a pledged slave who was freed owes nothing. Because of תיקון העולם, he is formally freed and writes a note for his value.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: no note, only freeing
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees and says no note is written. There is only the freeing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: He does not write a note; he only frees him.
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion in the משנה argues with the first one about writing the note.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion has two parts: freeing the slave and having him write a note. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל keeps only the freeing and drops the note, so in his view the slave takes on no debt.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
He does not write; he only frees.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a disagreeing opinion on the note-writing part of step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No note is written; there is only the freeing.

steps.title: Who freed the slave?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה and asks which master did the freeing.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: a slave whose master made him a designated payment and then freed him. Who freed him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its discussion by asking a clarifying question. The משנה said 'he freed him' but did not say who.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two people have a claim on the slave: the original owner, and the lender who holds him as payment. The question is which of them did the freeing, because that changes how we read the whole משנה.

phrases.english: GEMARA: A slave whose master made him a designated payment
and freed him: who freed him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for clarification of the case in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which master freed the slave: the original owner or the lender?

steps.title: רב: the first master freed him
steps.stepSummary: רב says the original owner freed the slave. So strict law means the slave owes nothing to the lender, called the 'second master.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: His first master freed him. The משנה means that by strict law the slave owes nothing to his second master.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers the question. It was the original owner who did the freeing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once we know the first master freed him, 'the slave owes nothing' gets a clear meaning: he does not have to serve the lender. The lender is called the 'second master' because he had a claim on the slave.

keyTerms.meaning: His first master, the original owner
His second master, here the lender who held him as payment

phrases.english: Rav said: his first master.
By the letter of the law the slave is not obligated
anything to his second master –
phrases.notes: The 'second master' is the lender, who had a claim on the slave because of the debt.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The original owner freed him, so by strict law the slave owes the lender nothing.

steps.title: רבא's rule: freeing cancels a lien
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why the slave owes the lender nothing, using רבא's rule. הקדש, חמץ and שחרור all cancel a lien.
steps.simpleTranslation: This follows רבא, who said: Consecrating something to the Temple, something becoming forbidden חמץ, and freeing a slave all cancel a lien.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up רב's reading with a known rule from רבא. It explains why strict law lets the slave go free of the lender.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A lender's claim (שיעבוד) on an item is normally strong. רבא teaches three things that are stronger and wipe out that claim, and freeing a slave is one of them. So once the first master frees the slave, the lender's claim on him is gone.

keyTerms.meaning: Consecrating something to the בית המקדש
A lien, a lender's legal claim on property

steps.whyThisMatters: רבא's rule shows that some changes in status are strong enough to cancel a lender's claim, which is why the משנה needs the חכמים' fix.

phrases.english: In accordance with Rava, as Rava said:
Consecration, leavened bread, and freeing –
remove an item from a lien;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source behind רב's statement that strict law frees the slave from the lender.
steps.raayaObject: That by strict law the freed slave owes nothing to the lender.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבא's rule that הקדש, חמץ and שחרור cancel a lien.

steps.title: Starting to explain the תיקון העולם reason
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to explain the משנה's 'but because of תיקון העולם.' The worry is that the lender might find the slave in the market.
steps.simpleTranslation: But because of the betterment of the world, in case he finds him in the market...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to explain the second half of the משנה, the חכמים' fix. The explanation only starts here and continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Strict law sets the slave free from the lender, so why do the חכמים step in? The גמרא starts to describe a worry: the lender might run into the slave in the market. The full concern is finished on the next amud.

phrases.english: But because of the betterment of the world,
lest he find him in the market
phrases.notes: 'He' is the lender, and 'him' is the freed slave. The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מִפְּנֵי תִּיקּוּן הָעוֹלָם, שֶׁמָּא יִמְצָאֶנּוּ בַּשּׁוּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After explaining strict law, the גמרא turns to the reason for the חכמים' fix.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The חכמים' fix exists because of a worry about the lender finding the freed slave in the market. The explanation continues on the next amud.
